However, the discovery of instances of actual confusion is not necessarily fatal to the application."}],"answer":"Yes—if information about actual confusion incidents is available, the Manual says the applicant should provide it, although such evidence is not usually provided to the examiner. This is Manual practice, not a statutory evidence requirement stated in this passage. [1]

If you do not know of any incidents, the Manual says applicants commonly include a brief statement to that effect in their declaration. That statement is taken at face value unless other circumstances cast doubt on its accuracy. A lack of knowledge is not the same as asserting that no confusion has ever occurred. [2]

If actual confusion is established, the Manual says it directly bears on the consideration of honesty and strengthens concerns about the likely degree of confusion. However, actual confusion is **not necessarily fatal to the application**. [3]
